Letting your listeners in on your process is one of the major gifts of any creative talk. Don't just walk people through your work. Take them on a journey that sparks curiosity and inspires new ideas. 2. The Dynamic Demo. If what you’re revealing is not just visual— like new technology or a novel invention— the audience wants to see it in action. Jeff Hahn demonstrated multi-touch technology in 2006, two years before the iPhone. Pranav Mistry demoed Six Sense technology, showing the possibilities when combining a phone, a projector, and a gesture-detecting camera. For a dynamic demo, what matters most is having something impressive to demonstrate. If it's truly compelling, you can excite your audience with a small tease about what they’re about to see. He poured muddy pond water, sewage runoff, and rabbit droppings into a container, then ran it through his Lifesaver bottle and offered it to an audience member. It tasted fine. He demonstrated that the technology worked, then explained its potential to save lives globally. A typical demo journey is: an initial tease, an explanation or context, the demo itself (visual and dramatic), then the significance— the impact it could have. Exceptional demos can become visions of the future. 3. The Dreamscape. Humans have the unique ability to imagine, invent, innovate, design, and envision worlds that don’t yet exist. We can share these visions, inspiring others to believe and act, and sometimes, turn them into reality. Screenwriters persuade studios to make movies. Inventors persuade companies to build inventions. Architects persuade clients to finance buildings. Businesspeople energize teams with belief in a new vision. Dreams can be communicated with images, demos, sketches, or words. Powerful speeches communicate a dream with inspiring language and passion.
